The harder question is what it actually costs — and whether we’re willing to pay it.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c08fd080415a7553051e0c", "tabs": [ "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4", "69c22206c7ede1d4fc6a5fa1", "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c085ddd46b33b7eed0d1f7", "69c0a0d2dad175912e825b7b", "69c09000d8c5e5cbe7c9eca5" ], "main-content": "

A few months ago I had a conversation that cost me something. A friend had said things that were unkind — not to me, but about someone I care about. I had a choice: ignore it, address it, or let it quietly end the friendship.

I chose to address it. The conversation went badly. There was no clean resolution. I walked away from it less certain about the friendship than I'd been before — and more certain that the honest thing is rarely the comfortable thing.

I think about that conversation when I read about Jesus on the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them. They don't know what they're doing.”

What strikes me is not the theology of the moment, though that's significant. What strikes me is the specificity. This is not a general posture of forgiveness toward people who wronged him in the past. This is forgiveness, spoken aloud, in the middle of being wronged. That's not idealism. That's a cost being paid in real time.

Paul writes, in his letter to the Philippians, about the pattern of Jesus: he had status and gave it up, took on the form of a servant, became obedient even when it led somewhere terrible. Not a passive state. An active choice to let go of something you could reasonably hold onto.

The honest thing is rarely the comfortable thing. Love at this level is not a feeling — it's a direction.

I am not very good at this. My instinct, when a relationship gets hard, is to protect myself — to manage my exposure, limit the damage, keep what I have. That's not always wrong. But it's also not the same thing as love.

There's a real question in here about limits. Does this mean we absorb every harm, endure every difficult person, never name what's true? I don't think so. Jesus didn't stay silent about what was wrong. Paul didn't pretend conflict didn't exist. Wisdom and love are not opposites.

But there is a version of self-protection that has nothing to do with wisdom — one that simply avoids the cost of caring about anyone inconvenient. And I notice that version in myself more than I'd like.

The conversation with my friend is still unresolved. I don't know where it ends. But I think the honest thing — and maybe the loving thing — was to stay in it rather than quietly walk away. That's a smaller thing than what Jesus describes. It might be the same kind of thing.
